strengths: The paper targets an important problem: exploiting known additive or junction-tree structure to improve optimization over large discrete scientific-design spaces.

Combining a factorized autoregressive search distribution with subtree-specific value functions is intuitive and potentially useful. The method can also be interpreted as structured credit assignment, suggesting applicability beyond proteins.

The experiments cover multiple sequence lengths, sample budgets, and protein-derived objectives. Several gains over the naive EDA are large, and the GB1 contact-threshold study usefully illustrates the trade-off between decomposability and predictive accuracy.
The manuscript is generally readable, with helpful figures, an explicit algorithm, and substantial appendix material.
weaknesses: The central derivation is incorrect. Equation 5, repeated as Equation 22, equates maximizing f with maximizing the sum of all Q-functions, but each parent Q-function already contains optimized descendant values, so this sum double-counts subtrees. In a two-node example with root-local value and child value (9,0) for state a and (0,8) for state b, f selects a because 9 exceeds 8, whereas Q_root plus Q_child selects b because 16 exceeds 9. Consequently, Equations 6/23 and the subsequent lower-bound argument do not establish equivalence to maximizing E[f]. A reward-to-go policy-gradient interpretation might rescue part of the algorithm, but that is not the proof presented and does not automatically justify the shaped weighted-MLE updates.

Algorithm 1 is not implementable as written: line 9 reuses the sample index and adds an unnormalized sum over all K child Q-values to every outer sample. This is neither the stated conditional expectation nor the usual same-trajectory Monte Carlo return, and would largely remove descendant-specific credit after mean centering. It is impossible to determine whether the experiments use this algorithm or a corrected version because code is unavailable.

Additional mathematical inconsistencies remain: the conditional EDA derivation drops a normalization constant that generally depends on the parent assignment, while the maximum-entropy derivation defines the soft value as log-sum-exp of Q even though temperature beta requires beta times log-sum-exp of Q divided by beta. The treatment of overlapping variables in junction-tree nodes is also only described informally in the implementation rather than defined consistently in the factorization.

The evaluation compares only against a single decomposition-unaware EDA. It lacks the closest factorized EDA baseline, a factorized-search ablation without messages, standard policy-gradient or return-to-go alternatives, and exact max-sum optimization where tractable. Thus the experiments do not isolate whether gains arise from message passing, factorization, architecture size, or ordinary local credit assignment.

The synthetic study uses only one sampled objective for each sequence length; the 20 repetitions vary initialization and sampling on the same objective and therefore do not establish performance across functions or tree structures. Because the single-variable tree instances admit efficient exact optimization, omitting optimality gaps is particularly problematic.

The protein experiments optimize the same learned, decomposition-constrained surrogate supplied to DADO. Predictive accuracy is largely unreported, generated sequences receive no independent or experimental evaluation, and mutation distances or other out-of-distribution diagnostics are absent. These results therefore demonstrate surrogate-score optimization, not the claimed practical scientific-design utility.

Parameter counts, wall-clock cost, component-evaluation cost, junction-tree sizes/treewidths, and selected hyperparameters are not reported. Hyperparameters are selected using final-iteration performance, but the use of held-out tuning seeds is unspecified. Statistical tests over seeds on fixed objectives and ambiguously defined confidence bands over sampled sequences overstate the breadth of evidence.

The reproducibility statement ends with “available publicly on GitHub:” but provides no URL. Important construction details and seeds are also missing. The manuscript additionally omits discussion of dual-use or biosecurity considerations associated with optimizing viral viability and protein sequences.

The alternative maximum-entropy derivation also has substantive errors. Its soft value should involve beta times log-sum-exp of Q divided by beta, and the proposed weighted-likelihood update does not correctly account for the entropy gradient.

The key comparison needed to support the contribution is absent: a tree-factorized search distribution trained using the global f(x) weight, or an FDA-like baseline. Other structured evolutionary or policy-gradient baselines are also missing.

These tests quantify stochastic variation on fixed landscapes rather than generalization across problems. Moreover, the pairwise tree objectives admit exact max-sum optimization, yet optimality gaps, regret, and exact-message-passing comparisons are omitted.

The protein experiments optimize the same deliberately decomposable learned surrogate used to construct DADO. They provide no assay validation, independent oracle, recovery of held-out high-fitness sequences, or uncertainty/OOD analysis. This is particularly serious because most underlying datasets contain almost exclusively single or double mutants while unconstrained optimization can propose distant sequences. Thus the claimed practical protein-design utility is unsupported.

The assertion of greater statistical efficiency has no variance, sample-complexity, convergence, or monotonic-improvement result. Parameter counts, runtime, component-evaluation cost, junction-tree sizes, and root sensitivity are also unreported.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised GitHub URL is missing; the synthetic epistasis construction contains a contradictory assignment; exact hyperparameter grids and selection/test separation are unclear; and selecting task-specific hyperparameters by final objective value risks optimistic comparisons.

The related-work discussion is too narrow for the novelty claim, especially regarding factored policy gradients, structured credit assignment, cooperative/gray-box evolutionary optimization, and arbitrary-graph multi-agent methods. No biosecurity or dual-use discussion is provided despite the protein and viral-capsid design applications.
